props.title: The Baby

sections.content: The Baby stands as one of the most disturbing psychological horror films of the 1970s, following social worker Ann Gentry (Anjanette Comer) as she investigates the bizarre case of "Baby" - a fully grown man kept in infantile state by his twisted family. Director Ted Post, known for mainstream fare like Beneath the Planet of the Apes (1970), takes an exploitation premise and crafts a genuinely unsettling examination of family dysfunction, control, and institutional power. The film shares DNA with other 1970s psychological horror classics like The Other (1972) and Don't Look Now (1973) in its exploration of family trauma and maternal obsession.

sections.content: The film emerged during a pivotal era of psychological horror that gave us The Exorcist (1973) and Don't Look Now (1973), when filmmakers were pushing boundaries in exploring family dynamics through a horror lens. What sets The Baby apart is its unflinching commitment to its premise - never playing it for camp despite its outlandish concept. The performances, particularly from Ruth Roman as the manipulative mother and David Mooney as Baby, walk a razor's edge between realism and Grand Guignol excess.

The film's themes of institutional care versus family bonds echo through later works like Mommy (2014) and We Need to Talk About Kevin (2011), though few dare to push into such extreme territory. The production design deserves special note - the Wadsworth family home becomes a character itself, with its dated décor and claustrophobic spaces reflecting the psychological imprisonment of its inhabitants. sections.content: While The Baby initially faced mixed reviews and controversy, its influence can be traced through later psychological horror films dealing with family dysfunction like Parents (1989) and Society (1989). The film's exploration of corrupted caregiving and maternal obsession presages works like The Hand That Rocks the Cradle (1992) and more recent films like Goodnight Mommy (2014).
